analysis.one_liner: Suspends most consumer debt collection — evictions, repossessions, utility shutoffs, lawsuits, and penalty fees — during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on March 23, 2020 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced three weeks into the pandemic, this bill would have barred debt collectors from repossessing cars, foreclosing, evicting tenants, shutting off utilities, garnishing wages, seizing bank funds, or suing over unpaid consumer debts while the COVID-19 emergency lasted. It would have also blocked late fees and penalty interest during that period, required lenders to extend loan terms by the number of payments missed, limited collection contact to written notices in English and Spanish, and voided forced-arbitration clauses for claims under the bill. To cover the cost to lenders, it would have directed the Federal Reserve to set up a facility compensating financial institutions for their losses. The bill went to the House Financial Services Committee and died there without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday borrowers behind on consumer debts — car loans, personal loans, utility bills, rent — during the pandemic. They would have been shielded from repossessions, evictions, shutoffs, lawsuits, wage garnishment, and late fees, and would have gotten extra time to repay afterward. Lenders would be reimbursed for their losses through the new Federal Reserve facility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers behind on debt during COVID

how_it_helps.text: During the COVID-19 emergency, debt collectors could not repossess cars, foreclose, evict tenants, shut off electricity, water, phone, or broadband service, or seize money from bank accounts or wages.
Collectors could not sue or threaten to sue over nonpayment, continue existing collection lawsuits, charge late fees, or raise interest rates because of missed payments.
After the emergency, collectors had to add missed payment periods back onto the end of the loan rather than penalize the borrower, and offer reasonable repayment plans or loan modifications.

Predispute arbitration agreements — contract clauses that force disputes into private arbitration instead of court — could not be used to block a consumer's claim under this bill, and violators faced civil liability of up to 10 times the normal amount.

Collection contact during the emergency was limited to written notices, clearly labeled as informational and provided in English and Spanish, so borrowers would not face constant collection calls while out of work.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, consumer lenders, debt collectors, landlords, and utility companies would have lost the ability to charge fees, raise rates, or force payment during the emergency — though a Federal Reserve facility would have compensated financial institutions for documented losses, spreading part of the cost to the public. Households would have faced the deferred debt after the emergency ended.

drawbacks.text: The bill extends the freeze to essentially all collection activity by all creditors — including landlords, utilities, and governments — during an emergency of indefinite length set by FEMA, which critics would say could leave small landlords and local utilities unable to cover their own bills for many months.
A temporary payment freeze can become a debt pile-up: missed payments are tacked onto the balance afterward, so households could face a large deferred bill once the emergency ends.
The Federal Reserve compensation facility for lenders' losses would put the government on the hook for the cost, effectively a public backstop for private loan books.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief to indebted households would have been immediate and large — no repossessions, evictions, shutoffs, lawsuits, or penalty fees for the duration of the emergency — and the bill's design tries to answer the obvious objection by compensating lenders through a Federal Reserve facility, though that shifts the cost onto the public. The main design risk is the deferred debt problem: a freeze delays, and in some ways enlarges, what households owe later. As drafted it is broad and would have been legally contested, but it was never amended, debated, or voted on, so its workability was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Joyce Beatty introduced the bill on March 23, 2020, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
It drew a single cosponsor, and no further action appears in its history — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and bills not passed by then expire; the bill never left committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer lenders, debt collectors, landlords, and utilities kept their full collection powers during the pandemic; no repossessions, evictions, shutoffs, or collection lawsuits were ever suspended by this bill.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat without action from March 23, 2020 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the single cosponsor were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill bars nearly all collection activity — lawsuits, garnishment, repossessions, late fees, penalty interest — on consumer debts (except mortgages) for the duration of the emergency. Unlike other versions of this idea, it would compensate lenders for documented losses through a new Federal Reserve facility, so the hit is softened but the industry's leverage over struggling borrowers is suspended.

The bill bars evictions during the emergency and defines any lessor of property as a creditor covered by its restrictions. Landlords would be unable to remove nonpaying tenants, with compensation only through the Fed facility if they are a loan holder.
The bill prohibits disconnecting electricity, gas, water, sewer, telephone, or broadband for nonpayment during the emergency. Companies would carry unpaid bills until the emergency ends.

The suspension of payments would cut off interest and fees, but the bill directs the Federal Reserve to establish a facility to pay covered institutions back for documented losses — so the government absorbs much of the cost.
The bill voids predispute arbitration clauses for claims brought under it, sending those disputes to court instead. This narrows a system that routinely makes consumer claims harder to pursue.
